title: OpenAI opens free GPT-5.6 Sol Pro access to 100,000 academic researchers by 2027
subtitle: The program starts with 10,000 selected researchers this summer and is part of a $250M commitment through 2027 to external science and discovery.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Academic Researchers on July 29, offering free access to its frontier models — including the GPT-5.6 Sol Pro tier — to selected researchers at academic institutions. The program starts with 10,000 participants this summer and is designed to reach 100,000 by 2027. Each selected researcher can invite four collaborators from the same institution, and participants receive roughly a year of access equivalent to the $200-per-month ChatGPT Pro tier. OpenAI framed the program as part of a broader $250 million commitment through 2027 to support external scientific research and discovery.

The mechanism matters more than the marketing. Sol Pro is currently OpenAI's flagship reasoning tier — the same model that OpenAI's own scientific teams use — and giving it away to researchers in biology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, mathematics, and physics puts frontier reasoning capacity directly in the hands of labs that otherwise could not afford to burn Pro-tier tokens on long-horizon exploration. That is a different distribution strategy than the science-focused vertical models Anthropic (Claude Science) and Google DeepMind have shipped this year, both of which are gated by paid contracts. OpenAI is essentially subsidizing scientific output in exchange for real-world evaluation signal on the model's usefulness in structured research.

The move fits a wider 2026 pattern of AI labs racing to embed frontier tools in scientific workflows: Insilico's rentosertib entered Phase III as the first fully AI-designed drug, Anthropic launched Claude Science and Claude for Teachers, and DeepMind published progress on prospective credit assignment for long-horizon agents. OpenAI is now the third major lab this year to build a large, subsidized science program — but at 100,000 researchers, it is the largest by headcount. The unresolved question is what happens to the outputs: OpenAI has not published detailed terms on IP, data retention, or whether the model will be trained on the research it helps produce.

For learners: if you are a graduate student, postdoc, or early-career researcher, applying is nearly free and the access is real. But read the terms of service carefully before feeding unpublished data into any hosted frontier model — retention and training-on-your-inputs policies vary widely between the science programs, and once your data leaves your machine, you cannot un-share it. This is the practical version of the AI-in-research debate: the tools are getting better and cheaper, and the discipline of knowing what to hand over lives entirely with you.
